ui.sheet_body: This is not your fault. Anacan will be by your side through this time.
ui.sheet_stop: Baby messages and pregnancy notifications will stop right away
ui.sheet_keep: Your album and chats are not deleted, just hidden
ui.sheet_date_sub: Recovery weeks are counted from this date
ui.sheet_partner_sub: We'll send them a gentle message and show them how to support you
ui.sheet_error: Something went wrong. Check your internet connection and try again.

ui.home_done_body: Recovery moves at a different pace for everyone. When you're ready, the options below will be waiting. There's no rush.
mood_reply: Today is very hard, and that's understandable. Don't push yourself to do anything. If you want, write to someone or talk to Anacan.AI.
Grief is love continuing. If you feel like crying, cry. These feelings will soften little by little.
Feeling empty is very common after a loss. Do one small thing today: drink some water, take a short walk, eat something.
Calm days happen too. Let yourself enjoy it, without feeling guilty.
Feeling better doesn't mean forgetting. Let yourself savor this moment.
ui.warn_title: See a doctor right away if you have:
ui.warn_body: heavy bleeding, a temperature above 38°C, severe pain, foul-smelling discharge or dizziness.

ui.p_card_title: Be by her side these days
ui.p_intro_body: This loss is hard for both of you. You have every right to grieve too. What matters most to her isn't finding the right words, it's you being there.

ui.p_hidden_note: Pregnancy missions, the birth plan and night shifts are temporarily hidden.

weeks.title: The first days
weeks.body: Bleeding and period-like cramps are normal this week. Use pads, not tampons. If the loss happened later in pregnancy, your breasts may produce milk: a snug bra and cold compresses help.
weeks.mind: Shock, sadness, anger, emptiness or feeling nothing at all — all of it is normal. The question “Why?” will come up a lot. This is not your fault.
todo: Rest and leave the housework to others
Keep an eye on your temperature and bleeding
Tell someone close how you're doing

weeks.title: Your body is healing
weeks.body: Bleeding usually eases, sometimes lasting 1–2 weeks. Drink plenty of water and eat iron-rich food (meat, lentils, spinach). Avoid pools, baths and sex until the bleeding stops.
weeks.mind: People around you are going back to life while you are still hurting. That gap can feel lonely. You don't need to hide your feelings.
todo: A short walk every day — only if you feel like it
Schedule the follow-up visit your doctor mentioned
Let your partner answer the questions that feel too heavy

weeks.title: Grief comes in waves
weeks.body: Tiredness may still linger. If the bleeding has stopped, gentle movement and a sleep routine help bring your strength back. A pregnancy test may stay positive for a few weeks, and that's normal.
weeks.mind: A hard day can follow a good one. Grief isn't a straight line. Seeing pregnant women and babies can be difficult — it's okay to protect yourself.
todo: Temporarily mute social media accounts that drain you
Talk about this with your partner
Do something small and kind for yourself

weeks.title: Rhythm returns
weeks.body: For many women, the body returns to its usual rhythm around these weeks. Your next period usually comes 4–6 weeks after the loss and may be a little different the first time.
weeks.mind: Getting back to daily life both helps and tires you. Don't rush back to work; if you can, lighten your load.
todo: Decide for yourself who at work you tell and how much
Note your mood once a day
If you need to, take the mood questionnaire (EPDS)

weeks.title: Small steps
weeks.body: Your energy is slowly coming back. Eat a balanced diet and talk to your doctor about taking folic acid. If you haven't had a follow-up visit yet, schedule it now.
weeks.mind: Dates — your due date, certain weeks — can feel heavy. Make a calm plan for those days ahead of time.
todo: Make a plan for the hard dates
Meet up with a friend
Choose gentle movement for your body: yoga, a walk

weeks.title: Remembering the love
weeks.body: Your body has mostly recovered. If your period hasn't come yet, talk to your doctor.
weeks.mind: Some families hold a small ritual of remembrance: writing a letter, planting a tree, lighting a candle. Only if you want to.
todo: Write a letter to them in My memories
Note what has been helping you
Spend time together with your partner

weeks.title: Coming back to yourself
weeks.body: Sleep, food and movement are the foundation of recovery. If you're thinking about a new pregnancy, decide together with your doctor when you're ready.
weeks.mind: Even as grief eases, it may not disappear completely. That means you haven't forgotten. If grief gets in the way of daily life for more than 2 weeks, talk to a specialist.
todo: Retake the mood questionnaire
Make one small plan for the future
Give yourself credit: you've made it this far

weeks.title: The road ahead
weeks.body: 8 weeks are behind you. Your body has recovered, but there's no time limit on your feelings.
weeks.mind: When you're ready, you can start tracking your cycle or move on to new plans. If you're not ready, that's okay too. Anacan won't rush you.
todo: Look at your options when you're ready
Thank the people who supported you
Come back to this guide whenever you need it

urgent: Heavy bleeding: soaking a pad completely within an hour
soon: My period still hasn't come after 8 weeks
Sadness or emptiness has been getting in the way of my daily life for more than 2 weeks
My sleep and appetite are completely disrupted

faq.a: No. Most early losses happen because of chromosomal differences in the baby, and no activity, stress, food or work causes them.
About 10–20% of confirmed pregnancies end in loss. You are not alone; people just rarely talk about it.

faq.q: When should I see a doctor?
faq.a: Right away if you have urgent signs. Otherwise, go to the follow-up visit your doctor scheduled and write down your questions beforehand.
Usually after 4–6 weeks. The first period may be heavier or lighter than usual. If 8 weeks have passed and it still hasn't come, see a doctor.

faq.q: Will this happen in my next pregnancy too?
faq.a: After one loss, most women go on to have a healthy pregnancy. If there have been repeated losses, your doctor may suggest additional tests.
It depends on how ready you feel, physically and emotionally. Decide on the timing together with your doctor; there's no need to rush.
There's no timetable for this. Grief softens as time goes by. If it gets in the way of daily life for more than 2 weeks, talking to a psychologist helps.

phases.title: The first days: be there
phases.body: Her body is healing through bleeding and pain, and her feelings are in shock. Don't search for the right words — being there is enough.
do: Take over the housework and meals completely
Tell the relatives yourself so she doesn't have to explain
Go to the doctor's appointment together
Keep an eye on her temperature and bleeding

phases.title: Weeks 3–4: the world moves on, she hasn't yet
phases.body: Everyone is going back to life, and you may feel it's already behind you. For her, grief keeps coming in waves.
do: Ask “How are you today?” every day and listen to the answer
Shield her from pregnant acquaintances and baby news

phases.title: Weeks 5–6: hard dates
phases.body: The due date or certain weeks may feel heavy for her. Know them in advance and be by her side.
do: Mark the hard dates in your calendar
If she wants to do something in remembrance, support her
Suggest calm plans to spend time together
Talk about your own grief too

phases.title: Weeks 7–8: moving forward together
phases.body: Her body is recovering, but the feelings may still continue. Discuss future plans at her pace.
do: Don't bring up a new pregnancy until she does
Prepare your questions for the doctor together
If needed, help her find a psychologist

say: Whatever you need, I'll do it.
If you want to cry, cry. I'm right here.
We will both never forget them.
avoid: “You should be over it by now.”
tasks: Let's go for a walk together this evening
I'm making you a warm cup of tea
phrases: I love you so much. I'm here 🤍
How are you today? Tell me whatever you need.
Don't do anything tonight, I've got it all.
I'm proud of you, you're so strong.
partner.you_body: Men often go through this loss in silence and hide their feelings because they think “I have to be strong.” But you have every right to grieve too. Grieving together brings you closer.
you_tips: Share your feelings with her too: “I'm sad too”
Talk to a friend you trust
Don't forget sleep, food and movement
If it gets hard, reach out to a psychologist
Don't drown your grief in alcohol or by escaping into work
